turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Near the balance wheel of some fine watches, you may see a thin, curved spring that looks like the neck of a swan. This part is called a swan-neck regulator, and it is both useful and beautiful.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: First, let's remember what a regulator does. The balance wheel swings back and forth, controlled by a hairspring. A small arm called the regulator can make the active part of the hairspring a little longer or shorter. This makes the watch run slower or faster.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The challenge is that the movements needed are tiny. Moving the regulator arm by just a fraction of a millimeter can change the timing by several seconds a day. With a simple arm, it is easy to push too far.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The swan-neck design solves this. The curved spring presses gently against one side of the regulator arm. On the other side, there is a fine micrometric screw. When the watchmaker turns this screw, the arm moves forward by a very small, controlled amount. The spring holds it firmly in place.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: This allows fine regulation, which means very precise adjustment. It also keeps the arm from slipping when the watch receives a knock.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Today, many watches use other systems. But the swan neck remains popular in traditional German and Swiss watches, because it shows that someone cared about both function and form.
